en: Preface to the Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. Written by the Grand Officer of the Middle Rank (Zhongshan Dafu),
Acting Censor-in-Chief (Shou Yushi Zhongcheng), Commissioner for Rectification and Inspection (Chong Lijianshi),
Acting Judge of the Interior Appointments of the Ministry of Personnel (Quanpan Liubu Liuneichuan), and Commander of the Upper Guard (Shang Hugun) of Langye Commandery.

Composed by Wang Sui, Marquis of Kaiguo, with a fief of one thousand nine hundred households (of which two hundred were actually held) and invested with the purple-gold fish pouch: *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Great Buddha-Usnīsa*. This work is the grand model of India and the precious scripture of the Garden of Dharma.

In the past, Śākyamuni emerged as the sovereign of the Five Indias and the sole honored one within the Three Realms; he utilized the Golden Wheel to initiate all beings and manifested the Jade Tuft to respond to the world. Observing the suffering endured by the four classes of birth, he bestowed compassionate relief upon all creatures;
pitying that the various capacities of sentient beings had not yet awakened, he exerted himself to provide skillful guidance.

Thereupon, he contemplated the ultimate truth and expounded the subtle words; he opened the gate of great compassion and broadened the ocean of *tathatā*. He maintained that all phenomena arise solely in dependence upon deluded thoughts, and that all sentient beings exist only through causes and conditions.
Thus he realized that the cycle of birth and death has greed and desire as its root, while the cultivation and realization of eternal bliss take meditative wisdom as their essence.

Thus, this scripture can distinguish and identify various māras and destroy the seven realms of existence; it teaches the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to cultivate the wondrously luminous mind of the Perfect Teaching;
it inspires the true awakening that returns to the source, and realizes the discourse on the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Vehicle.
Yi (Wang Yi) translated its meaning from the Bala language, while Fang (Xuanlao) and Xiang (Yu) composed its prose.

Now, the Dharma Master Faquan of Jiangwu is preeminent both in learning and insight, possessing unimpeded eloquence. Taking this scripture as the teaching for his era within a single dispensation, he analyzes its wondrous principles through ten gates. His merit rescues the great chiliocosm, and his Way transmits the non-dual truth. By fixing his gaze and joining his palms, he clarifies delusion; by destroying appearances and dissolving the mind, he reunites with the source. To believe and accept it is to become a bridge and raft for the world; to achieve awakening through it is to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Thus, by manifesting the sutras through the commentaries and clarifying the principles through the commentaries, one can resolve prior doubts and settle subsequent obstructions, strip away the clouds of delusion to behold the sun of wisdom. Only then does one realize that form and emptiness are no different, both returning to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
and that sentient beings and Buddhas are not distinct, for they do not depart from the square inch of the mind.

Having followed my inclination to provide external protection and, out of a sense of shame, having failed to engage in internal study, I have nonetheless had the opportunity to peruse this work; I have therefore composed this preface and introduction, taking refuge in the Jewel of the Dharma, hoping that you will diligently investigate its true meaning.
I praise the Buddha Vehicle, wishing that its supreme fruits may universally benefit all beings.

On the twenty-first day of the first month of winter in the eighth year of the Tiānshèng era of the Great Song (the Gēngwǔ year of the Qīnglóng cycle), on the *xīnchōu* day, this preface for the East Porch of the Dàozhāi was respectfully submitted by the Tripitaka Master of the Translation Bureau, Cháo-sàn-dàfū, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Grand Master of Radiant Dharma, the Purple-Robed Venerable Wéijìng, to the Honorable Vice-Minister of the Censorate.

I have recently received the newly composed "Preface to the Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra," which you have graciously bestowed upon me. That great scholars and eminent sages praise this precious vehicle, and that those of shallow learning and the monastic community may glimpse its dharma-words, brings such joy to my body and mind and increases the clarity of my all-encompassing wisdom. Receiving it with the highest reverence and taking refuge in it, I am overcome with immeasurable gratitude.

I humbly submit that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas—is the gateway to the practices of bodhisattvas and the heart-seal of all Buddhas. It reveals that conditioned phenomena are, from the outset, the wondrous functions of the sands of the Ganges; it shows that returning to the signless is the true source of the Dharma-realm. It is neither existent nor empty, transcending names and forms beyond the reach of words and expressions;
it manifests causes and demonstrates fruits, and distinguishes the stages and positions within the midst of spiritual transformations.

Objects do not obstruct the mind, and delusions do not obstruct wisdom. The nature of the seven great elements is so vast that it depends on nothing; the principle of the eight returns is such that they have no source from which they return.

Thus, one realizes the mind of True Suchness, brings to rest the root of delusion, gives rise to the wisdom of skillful means, and proclaims the secret words. By this, the myriad dharmas are made perfectly interfused, and all Buddhas attain sovereign mastery. Entering the two truths within non-duality and awakening to the three emptinesses as non-empty—sublime indeed is the True Teaching, inconceivable!

There was a man of lofty character who composed commentaries and treatises, brilliantly elucidating the secret interpretations and concisely discussing the Buddha’s intent. We respectfully consider how you, Excellency, have entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and understood the causes and conditions of the Dharma; you have studied the Buddha’s practice to dispel the maladies of existence and emptiness, proclaiming the nature and characteristics of phenomena while harmoniously clarifying the source of arising and ceasing. You act as a guardian of the city of the Dharma and serve as an uninvited friend.
This high-quality preface elucidates the vehicle of the teachings, establishing a model for all generations and providing a torch for those in the eternal darkness.
Having long been favored by the Master’s spiritual regard, I have had the honor of perusing these extraordinary writings; overwhelmed by his kindness, I cannot restrain my joy.
Not to be circulated.
Respectfully submitted by Wei Jing.

2. The Collection by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui on Deliverance from Māra through Other-Power. This is intended to assist those with heavy obstacles by means of the power of mantras.
Section Two:
Exposition of the Meaning in Brief, Part One: A General Summary of the Previous Text. (Four subsections:
1. A General Summary of the Previous Text.
“Ānanda! Regarding your question on gathering the mind, I shall first explain the wondrous gateway for training in the entry into samādhi.

Those who seek the Bodhisattva path must first maintain these four kinds of discipline as pure as ice and frost; then, the various branches and leaves—namely, the three types of mental misconduct and the four types of verbal misconduct—will naturally fail to arise, for their birth would have no cause.”
Ānanda! If these four matters are not lost, the mind will not even take form, sound, smell, taste, or touch as its object; how then could any demonic activities arise?

The precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation; by relying on these precepts, one attains concentration and wisdom. Therefore, it is known that samādhi takes the precepts as its primary manifestation.
Although these grave prohibitions pertain to body and speech, each and every one of them governs the mind.

Since one is already in accord with meditative concentration and wisdom, form, fragrance, taste, and touch are none other than the true mark (dharmatā); how could there be demonic activities to disturb or confuse the practitioner?
Second, exhorting the recitation of divine mantras.

"If there are those whose past habitual tendencies cannot be extinguished, you should teach such people to single-mindedly recite my supreme divine mantra, the *Mahā-sātrapatra* from the Radiant Light of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa."

"This is the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown; the Buddha of the Unconditioned Mind radiates brilliance from the crown, and this heart-mantra is proclaimed while seated upon a precious lotus flower.
Although it was previously explained at length that maintaining pure precepts is as bright as ice and frost, by not creating new karma, one has already distanced oneself from the affairs of Māra.

However, there are stains and obstructions from beginningless past habits, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which follow the body like a shadow and hinder the Way. For the practitioner, these act as obstacles at all times: they may manifest as frequent illness and affliction, excessive lust and anger, encountering false teachers, or being disturbed by demons; various difficulties arise in competition. All of these are the manifestation within consciousness of the seeds of unwholesome karma and distorted thoughts from beginningless past causes, which constantly act as enemies to the Right Path.

Ordinary beings who have only recently begun their training possess weak powers of the Path and are unable to dispel [obstacles]; therefore, the Buddha possesses sublime mantras that can extinguish the evil habits of past lives, ensuring they are not afflicted by disturbances, so that the power of the Path may be swiftly perfected without encountering retreat or discouragement.

It was previously stated that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) destroy the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and it was further clarified that the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) merely halts sinful karma; now it is taught that divine mantras (*vidyā-mantra*) can destroy past calamities while simultaneously eliminating the obstructions of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
If the three obstacles are indeed eliminated, what need is there to wait for realization?
Third, pointing out the efficacy of the practice:

"Furthermore, your karmic conditions with Mātanga over kalpas of past lives—your habits of affectionate attachment have not been formed in a single lifetime or a single kalpa; yet as soon as I proclaimed [the truth], your love was forever severed and you became an Arhat."
That courtesan had no intention to practice, yet through the secret assistance of spiritual power, she swiftly realized the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

How much more so for you, Śrāvakas assembled here, who seek the Supreme Vehicle and are certain to attain Buddhahood? It is like raising dust in a favorable wind; what difficulty or danger could there be?
"Tiṅga had the habit of lust in her past lives; that she has now attained freedom from desire is the severing of the obstacle of karmic afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
She currently manifests as a courtesan, yet she has now attained the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*); this is the transformation of the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*)."

If even those who practice without a focused mind can attain the fruits of sainthood upon encountering this divine mantra, how much more so for those who aspire to the path of unsurpassed enlightenment and practice with determination! With the empowerment of the mantra’s power, what perils could possibly prevent them from reaching their goal?
IV. A Brief Indication of the Method for Upholding [the Precepts], in two parts:
1. Indicating the Ritual Practice.

"If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they must first uphold the pure prohibitory precepts of a bhikṣu. They must certainly select a foremost śramaṇa whose precepts are pure to serve as their teacher; if they do not encounter a truly pure monk, your ritual of the precepts will certainly not be perfected."

After the precepts have been completed, one should don new, pure garments, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion; recite this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times, and then perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), establish the *maṇḍala*, and pray that the Unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions will emit the light of great compassion and pour it upon one’s crown.

"If one's observance of the precepts is incomplete, even the five conditions will be lacking; how much more so when acting as a teacher or model to transmit them to others—if one's own precepts are impure, how can the precepts of others be established?"
Therefore, one must select a foremost, pure, and authentic preceptor for bestowing the precepts.
Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If there is no preceptor to bestow the precepts within a thousand li, one should receive the precepts by making a vow before the Buddha oneself."

First repent for the seven heinous offenses, and afterwards seek the dharma of the precepts; only when you behold auspicious signs shall you know that your offenses have been extinguished and the precepts obtained—otherwise, they cannot be attained.

Once the precepts are accomplished, dwell in a quiet and secluded place, burning incense and reciting mantras one hundred and eight times to symbolize the eradication of the one hundred and eight afflictions.

Internal precepts and external mantras are employed to prevent the arising of māras; fearing that they might obstruct the ritual site (maṇḍala), one must first seek the empowerment of the manifest Buddhas’ illuminating light. Thus, the mind attains valor, and progress on the Path becomes even more rapid.
2. Clarifying Response and Resonance. "Ānanda!

If, in such an age of decline, there are pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or lay donors who extinguish greed and lust in their hearts, uphold the Buddha’s pure precepts, and within a place of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) make the vows of a bodhisattva; who bathe upon entering and leaving, and practice the Way during the six periods of the day and night without sleep for twenty-one days—then I shall personally manifest my body before that person, stroke their head to comfort them, and cause them to attain awakening."

The sequence of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the performance of the ritual protocols are as described in Guifeng Shan’s *Ritual for the Cultivation and Realization of Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué xiūzhèng yí*).
Reciting mantras to bestow empowerment and making vows to behold the Buddha, such that the Buddha manifests his body, is termed "responsive resonance" (*ganying*).
If one perceives other objects, turning away from one's original practice such that events contradict one's aspirations, this is a realm of Māra and not a true response.
Furthermore, when perceiving the True and the Responsive, the mind attains awakening, afflictions become thin and sparse, and wisdom becomes bright and pure.

If, upon seeing the Buddha, one remains as dull-witted as before and even finds afflictions increasing, these are all demonic realms and not the true Buddha. 1. Inquiry. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already attained awakening; I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

In this age of the final dharma, when practitioners establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), how should they perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) in accordance with the pure regulations of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?

"I have lived in the Buddha’s world and received the Buddha’s personal instruction; now, having attained awakening, I know that through cultivation and realization one will surely reach the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

For those who study during the Dharma-ending age (*mofa*), how can they apply themselves with greater effort and establish a site for the Way (*daochang*)? What methods are there to ensure their practice follows the proper rules?"
II. The Response and Explanation, in two parts:
A. Showing the method for binding the maṇḍala, in two parts:
1. The dimensions of the maṇḍala site.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If people of the末世 (final age) wish to establish a *bodhimaṇḍa*, they should first procure a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the lush, fatty fragrant herbs of those mountains."
These oxen drink only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; their dung is fine and fragrant, and one may take this dung and mix it with sandalwood to smear upon the ground.
Were they not from the Snowy Mountains, the oxen would be foul-smelling and filthy, unfit for smearing upon the ground.

Apart from the level plain, dig into the earth to a depth of five feet or more and take the yellow soil. Mix it with the ten kinds of incense—Uśīra, Agallochum, Sūkṣma, Turuṣka, Kuṅkuma, Sarjarasa, Devadāru, Jātī, Tagara, and Kakkola—and grind these ten ingredients into a fine powder. Combine this with the soil to form a paste, which is then used to coat the ground; a square of sixteen feet is made into an eight-cornered altar.

"The milk of the snow-mountain cows is pure *sarpis* (clarified butter); all their dung is most fragrant and clean, and by mixing it with a single measure of sandalwood, it may be used to smear the ground."
If these [materials] are unavailable, one should instead take deep soil and mix it with ten kinds of various fragrant substances to smear upon the site.

The eight-cornered altar, whether square or circular, should be made according to the prescribed measurements by excavating the ground; it should have no tiered steps, as is the case with the *xian* (sacrificial mounds) used today.
Although the altar has eight corners, it is divided into ten sections above and below to correspond with the number of the circle.

This is because the subsequent text mentions the hanging of mirrors facing one another, with light intermingling from above and below; within each mirror, the Buddhas of the ten directions appear, symbolizing that one body is ten bodies and ten bodies are one body—repeatedly and infinitely, mutually manifesting and mutually containing one another.
This signifies the marks of the inconceivable realm of the *cittaprakṛti* (storehouse consciousness).
In the following passage, where the Buddhas of the ten directions appear simultaneously with their mirrors reflecting one another’s light, this is precisely that mark.
II. The Ritual for Making Offerings, in two parts:
A. Listing the Offering Utensils, in two parts:
1. Utensils for Long-Term Use.

"At the center of the altar, place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood; upon the flower, set a bowl; within the bowl, first fill it with dew collected during the eighth month, and within the water, place whatever flowers and leaves are available."

Take eight round mirrors and place each in its respective direction, surrounding the flower bowl; outside the mirrors, establish sixteen lotus flowers, with sixteen incense burners interspersed among the flowers and arranged as an adornment, burning only aloeswood incense so that the flames are not visible.

Take the milk of white cows and place it in sixteen vessels; from this milk, prepare pancakes, along with various granulated sugars, oil cakes, milk porridge, *sugandhaka* honey-ginger, pure clarified butter, and pure honey. Arrange these, each in sixteen portions, surrounding the outside of the lotus flower, and offer them to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not eat this food; rather, they manifest eating it in order to increase merit, so that practitioners may become fully endowed with merit and wisdom and swiftly attain perfection.
Just as the Buddha accepted Cunda’s final offering so that he might fulfill the *dānapāramitā*, this case is likewise; therefore, one must make offerings.
Second, offerings according to the occasion.

"Whenever it is mealtime or at midnight, take half a *śoṇa* of honey and three *śoṇas* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Before the altar, separately install a small fire hearth; boil *turuṣka* incense to produce scented water and wash the charcoal with it, then ignite it until it blazes fiercely."
"Cast this ghee and honey into the blazing furnace, burning them until the smoke is exhausted, to offer as a sacrifice to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Second, regarding the arrangement of images:

"Have banners and flowers suspended everywhere on the four exterior sides, and within the altar chamber, install the images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions upon the four walls."

One should display images of Vairocana, Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, and Amitābha facing directly forward; furthermore, various great transformational forms of Avalokiteśvara, together with Vajragarbha, should be placed at their left and right sides.

Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma along with Lambodara, the various Guhyakas together with Bhṛkuṭī, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pinnayaka were stationed at the sides of the gate, arranged on the left and right.

Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them in the air, facing the mirrors installed within the ritual mandala, so that their forms and reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers.

"Hang banners and arrange images so that each one casts its reflection in a mirror; by causing practitioners to become thoroughly familiar with this realm, they will find it easy to realize the principle of the Dharma-realm of non-obstruction among all phenomena."

Whether in time or place, within a single thought-moment, one travels throughout the ten directions, perceives all Buddhas everywhere, performs all Buddha-works everywhere, and receives offerings everywhere.
As it is with a single thought-moment, so it is in every atom of dust.
II. Clarifying the Ritual Procedures for Reciting Mantras, in two parts:
A. Clarifying the Practice, in three parts:
1. Cultivating Auxiliary Practices.

"During the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity pay homage to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the title of Arhat; constantly reciting mantras around the altar during the six periods of the day and night, one should practice the Way with a sincere heart, performing one hundred and eight repetitions at each session."

During the second seven-day period, one should single-mindedly and exclusively resolve upon the Bodhisattva vows with an uninterrupted mind; in my Vinaya, there is already a teaching on the practice of such vows.

During the third seven-day period, one should single-mindedly maintain the Buddha’s *pāṇḍaravāsini* (Bhr̥kuṭī) mantra throughout the twelve periods of the day and night. Upon reaching the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will simultaneously appear at the place where mirrors reflect one another's light, and one shall receive the Buddhas’ empowerment by the touching of their crowns.
During the twenty-one days, the practices performed were each distinct.

At the outset, one prostrated before the Buddha, circumambulated the altar, recited mantras, and practiced the Way; within this period, one must certainly perform the Five Repentances (pañca-pratikramaṇa), prostrating before the Buddha to seek his compassionate empowerment for repentance, thereby severing the obstacle of pride (*māna-āvaraṇa*) and so forth.
Next, one should relinquish what was previously practiced and constantly make great vows; thus, one directs the mind toward vastness and leaves behind the obstacles of narrowness and inferiority.
Finally, one should single-mindedly recite and maintain the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*), employing the gate of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to ward off all demonic activities.

Through the power of these three limitations aiding one's cultivation, the path of response and resonance intersects, whereby he manifests the Buddha’s response by placing his hand upon [the practitioner’s] head to offer comfort.
Second, entering contemplative practice:
"One immediately cultivates *samādhi* within the site of enlightenment, enabling those who study and practice in this degenerate age to have bodies and minds as clear and pure as lapis lazuli."

Once the demonic obstacles have been removed and one further receives the manifest empowerment, one practices samādhi and swiftly attains accomplishment; thus, the body and mind become as clear and pure as lapis lazuli.
Third, showing that it is not accomplished: "Ānanda!
If among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor and the ten bhikṣus of the assembly, even one is impure, then such a site of practice will for the most part not be accomplished."
The root of the precepts is the foundation and the primary gateway for entering the Way; both the teacher and the witness must be equally pure.
If the teacher has any deficiency, the disciple has no one to inherit [the lineage]; thus, the site of enlightenment cannot be established—this is the reason for such a requirement.
2. Clarifying the Attainment of the Fruit.
"After three weeks, he sat upright in meditative retreat for one hundred days.

Those of sharp faculties attained the stage of Srotāpanna without rising from their seats; even if their physical and mental bodies had not yet fully realized the holy fruit, they knew with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood would be unerring."
"You have asked about the site of enlightenment; it is established in this manner.

While the fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-entry) is a term common to both the Great and Small Vehicles—the latter being well known—since one is now practicing the Mahayana *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and generating the bodhisattva vows, the fruits should be discussed according to the stages of the Mahayana.

According to the *Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Garland* (*Yingluo benye jing*), "the first stage is called *kumārabhūta*, up to the fourth stage which is called *srotāpanna*, and the Buddha-stage is called *bhagavān buddha*."
If one were to correlate this with the present sutra, I fear it might be too profound.

However, if we consider the realization of the Truth and the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) as being named *srotāpanna*, this is most fitting; it corresponds precisely to the initial entry into the stages of abiding (*vihāra*) within the distinct (*byō*) and perfect (*en*) teachings. This is exactly identical in meaning to the practice and realization of Avalokiteśvara.

If one were to assign this to a lower stage, it would likely be inappropriate, for this sutra refers to it as the "sage-fruit" (āryaphala) and states that it is cultivated by those of sharp faculties.

Furthermore, since the subsequent sutra mentions attaining the patience of non-arising (anutpattikadharmakṣānti), it is already realized at the third gradual stage; thus, there is no contradiction. One must certainly not assign it to an unattained stage; please examine this carefully.

1. The inquiry, in three parts:
1. A description of receiving the power of the mantra.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to him:
“Since I left the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s affectionate fondness; because I sought extensive learning, I have not yet realized the unconditioned.”
"Having encountered the prohibitions of that Brahmā’s evil arts, although my mind was clear, my power was not free.
It was by relying on meeting Mañjuśrī that I attained liberation.

Although Ānanda had attained the first fruit of the Hīnayāna, from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, it is called "provisional analytical cessation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) rather than true unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); therefore, it is said that he had not yet realized [the ultimate].
2. We pray to hear the words of the mantra.
"Although we have secretly obtained the power of this Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa Divine Mantra, we have not yet heard it directly.

We only pray that the Greatly Compassionate One will proclaim it once more, out of pity to rescue all those practicing in this assembly, as well as those in saṃsāra in the future; by receiving the Buddha’s secret voice, may their bodies and minds attain liberation."
Mañjuśrī silently recited [the verse] to resolve the difficulty regarding sexual misconduct; therefore, he said, "I have not heard it.
His current request for an explicit exposition is intended solely for its transmission to future generations.

Third, the benefits of upholding the mantra: those who uphold this mantra shall be protected by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and they will never fall into the evil realms. Furthermore, they will attain long life, freedom from illness, and the fulfillment of all their aspirations. Thus ends the third part, the instruction on the ritual methods for reciting the mantra. Fourth, the entrustment of the teaching: the Buddha addressed the assembly, saying, "You should all diligently uphold and propagate this secret mantra, so that all sentient beings may obtain peace and happiness. Fifth, the conclusion: having spoken these words, the Tathāgata entered the samādhi of the Dharma-realm, and the entire assembly, filled with joy, respectfully received and practiced the teaching. Thus ends the second chapter, "The Secret Mantra."
First, the manifested Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred-jeweled light from his uṣṇīṣa. From within this light, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses emerged, upon which manifested Tathāgatas sat amidst the precious flowers. From their crowns, ten streams of hundred-jeweled radiance issued forth; each stream of light universally manifested ten *gaṅgā*-sands of Vajrapāṇis, who bore mountains and held vajras, pervading the entire realm of empty space.

The great assembly looked up in reverence, harboring both fear and love; seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection, they listened with single-minded devotion as the Tathāgata Amitābha (the One Whose Crown Cannot Be Seen Emitting Light) proclaimed the divine mantra.

It shall now be explained that the divine mantra manifests radiance and transforms into Buddhas, and these transformations further produce emanations as numerous as the sands of hundreds of Ganges Rivers.
This is precisely the inconceivable, wondrous function of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind: the one is all, and the all is one.
The great assembly is about to realize this principle; therefore, it is manifested as a sign.
What follows is the exposition of the divine mantra, which serves as the secret cause for this realization; it is proclaimed to the assembly to transform others and bring them benefit.

"Ban (26) Svāhā (427). This mantra consists of four hundred and twenty-seven phrases.

The preceding counts of phrases merely consist of taking refuge in the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and various worthy sages, as well as describing the empowerment of the mantra's vows to bring about liberation from all evil spirits, diseases, and other calamities.

At the four hundred and nineteenth [verse], it says "tadyathā," which means "it is said as follows, namely, the mantra. From the syllable "oṃ" at the four hundred and twentieth [verse] onward is the actual mantra.
As previously stated, one should practice the Way and recite mantras during the six periods of the day, reciting this heart-mantra exactly one hundred and eight times for each period;
it would be even more excellent if one were to recite them all together.
However, this is precisely the secret Śūraṅgama; it has not been translated since antiquity for five general reasons:
first, it consists of the esoteric speech and secret dharma of all Buddhas, which is understood only by Buddhas communicating with Buddhas, and cannot be fully comprehended by other sages;
second, it is a door of dhāraṇī, as each individual word and phrase contains manifold meanings, just as the term Bhagavat possesses six kinds of meanings.
Third, it may be the name of a king of the *pretas*; by invoking it, one commands him to protect the practitioner.

Fourth, it is the secret seal (*mudrā*) of all Buddhas; like a royal seal of authority, there is nowhere it does not penetrate, and both the hidden and the manifest worlds revere it. Transmitted from Buddha to Buddha, it must not be altered. Fifth, it is sustained by the power of inconceivable majesty (*adhiṣṭhāna*);

merely reciting it secretly can extinguish great transgressions and lead one swiftly to the rank of the sages. It is like a king bestowing great grace and pardoning even those facing execution: those with merit are promoted and appointed to office, and this [mantra] is likewise.
Therefore, since ancient times, it has not been permitted to provide commentaries on this text.

Although there may be some differences between its various versions, these are merely variations in terminology regarding the "three periods," "treasuries," "middle," and "edges," as well as minor discrepancies in translation; one should simply rely on a single version for recitation and upholding, without attempting to choose between them.
II. Narrating the Efficacy of the Mantra, in two parts:
A. Clarifying that all Buddhas uphold it, in three parts:
1. The virtues achieved by those who uphold it, in three parts:
First, the aspect of attaining Buddhahood, subduing Māra, and preaching the Dharma:
"Ānanda, these subtle and wondrous verses and phrases of the *Śrī-Usṇīṣavijaya-sitātapatrā-rahasya-gāthā* give birth to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions."
By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By holding this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions subdue all māras and restrain all heterodox teachers.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, mounting this mantra-heart, sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, containing this mantra-heart, turn the Great Dharma Wheel within lands as numerous as motes of dust.
*Śītātapatrā* means "White Parasol," which refers to the hidden mind (*garbha-citta*).
It is called "white" because it is not associated with deluded defilements;
it is called a "parasol" because it universally covers all phenomena.
From this, secret divine mantras have flowed forth; hence it is called the "Mantra-Mind" (dhāraṇī-hṛdaya).

Furthermore, because it is the essential core of all mantras, there is not a single Buddha who has not attained perfect enlightenment by means of this mantra, nor who has not subdued all demons and heretics, responded to various lands, and turned the Great Wheel of Dharma.
2. The characteristics of the Master’s bestowing of the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) and the removal of suffering:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions hold this mantra-heart; they can bestow predictions by touching [the crown of the head] in the ten directions.
Even before one's own fruition is accomplished, one also receives the Buddha's prediction in the ten directions."

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions rely upon this mantra-heart to rescue and deliver sentient beings from suffering throughout the ten directions—namely, the sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; the suffering of being blind, deaf, or mute; the suffering of meeting those one hates, the suffering of parting from those one loves, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and the blazing intensity of the five aggregates. All manner of calamities, both great and small, are simultaneously liberated: the perils of bandits, armies, kings, and prisons; the perils of wind, fire, and water; and hunger, thirst, and poverty—all dissolve away as soon as they are thought of.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-heart, are able to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions; within the four modes of deportment, they make offerings as they wish, and among the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they are promoted to the rank of Great Dharma Prince.
Bestowing predictions brings about happiness; removing hardships uproots suffering.

Serving and making offerings as a prince of the Dharma is to succeed the Dharma King, ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed—all of this is made possible through the power of the mantra-heart.
3. The Section on Gathering Kinsmen, Manifesting Extinction, and Entrusting the Dharma.

"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this mantra-heart; it can gather and sustain their close kinsmen throughout the ten directions, causing those of the Hīnayāna who hear this secret treasury not to give rise to alarm or fear."
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite this mantra-heart and attain unsurpassed enlightenment; they sit beneath the Bodhi tree and enter Great Nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart, entrusting the affairs of the Buddha-dharma after their parinirvāṇa, so that it may be maintained to the ultimate end, and the precepts are strictly purified, all becoming perfectly clean.

After the four meals, all the sons and their remaining kinsmen attained the state of renunciation; having realized the Small Vehicle and heard the Great Vehicle, they were neither startled nor terrified.

That he, through the power of his compassionate gathering, manifested the attainment of Buddhahood and its subsequent passing away to entrust the future so that my Way would not fall to the ground—all this was none other than the efficacy of the mantra.
The efficacy of the span of two fingers:

"If I were to recite this Buddha-Crown Radiant Mass Pañcara mantra from dawn until dusk, with the sounds linked continuously and the syllables and phrases never overlapping, it could not be exhausted even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The secrets are inexhaustible and their efficacious power is never-ending.
Even if one were to speak for the duration of a kalpa, continuing day after day, it could not be fully described.
Third, there is no holding of faults.

"This mantra is also called the 'Crown of the Tathāgata. For you who are still in training and have not yet exhausted saṃsāra, if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship, it is impossible that you could sit in the place of practice without holding this mantra and thereby distance your body and mind from all demonic activities."
This mantra subsumes the secret treasury of all Buddhas and is complete with the myriad practices; therefore, it is impossible for a student to attain the Way without upholding this mantra.
2. Exhorting sentient beings to receive and uphold [the teaching], in three parts:
first, the general exhortation to receive and uphold.
"Ānanda!..."

In whatever worlds there may be, according to the specific lands and the sentient beings therein, one should write this mantra on birch bark, palm leaves, paper, or white cotton cloth produced in those respective countries, and store it within a fragrant pouch.
If this person’s mind is dull such that they are unable to recite it from memory, whether they carry it upon their person or write it within their home,
you should know that throughout their entire life, they cannot be harmed by any poisons whatsoever.
Since there is no inherent nature for recitation, merely copying, wearing, and maintaining [this mantra] will ensure that the various poisons produced throughout one's life can never cause harm.
Second, the specific explanation of its efficacy has two parts:
first, the heading.
“Ānanda! I shall now further explain this mantra for you, which protects and delivers the world, grants great fearlessness, and brings about the supramundane wisdom of all beings.”
2. Explanation, in eleven parts:
1. Ability to eliminate all calamities.

"If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite this themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such sentient beings who uphold it through recitation cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by great or small poisons. Furthermore, no evil spells of dragons, devas, ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, or *mārās* can take hold of them, and their minds will attain right concentration (*samādhi*)."

All curses, malevolent sorcery, poisons—whether from gold, silver, plants, trees, insects, snakes, or the poisonous vapors of myriad things—that enter this person’s mouth shall turn into the flavor of nectar.
All malevolent stars and various ghosts and spirits who harbor cruel hearts and seek to harm people will be unable to give rise to evil toward such a person.
The Vināyakas, the various evil kings of ghosts, and their retinues, having all received profound kindness, shall constantly provide protection.

Various poisonous and malevolent spirits, as well as the difficult circumstances of the world, cannot assail them; those who have attained right concentration (samādhi) are protected by the pervasive majesty of the divine spirits and the compassionate care [of the Buddha], whereby they obtain benefit and, in gratitude for this profound kindness, constantly provide protection.
Second, it is capable of generating all wisdoms.

"Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is always accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*-koṭis of the family of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas; each one has a retinue of vajra-beings who attend upon them day and night."

If there are sentient beings who, with a distracted mind and not in a state of samādhi, merely recollect and maintain this in their speech, the Vajra King will constantly follow those sons of good family; how much more so for those who possess the resolute bodhicitta.
The refined essence of these Vajra Bodhisattvas, the King of the Treasury, is subtle and swift; it awakens their spiritual consciousness.
At that moment, this person’s mind is able to remember eighty-four thousand Ganges-sand eons, knowing them thoroughly and without any doubt.
"If even those who recite with a distracted mind receive such protection, how much more so will those who seek Bodhi with a resolute mind not be granted their protection!

Since the Bodhisattva’s refined essence has already secretly permeated their consciousness, they will swiftly attain awakening; they will naturally remember events from kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, knowing them all without exception."
"Yin" (陰) means darkness, and it also implies a swift summoning.
It refers to being darkly influenced by karmic resonance, which causes [the faculties] to open and develop.
Third, one does not fall into evil realms.

"From the first kalpa until their final body, in every successive birth they shall not be born as yakṣas, rākṣasas, or pūtanas; nor as kaṭapūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, or piśācas, nor among any of the hungry ghosts—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—in such evil states."

If these good sons read, recite, copy, transcribe, wear, or preserve it, and offer various material offerings, they shall not be born into poverty, lowliness, or unpleasant states throughout kalpa after kalpa.
"The first kalpa" refers to the initial stage of generating the resolve and beginning practice.
Reaching until the time of the Bodhisattva’s final existence, it is therefore called the "final body.

Throughout this interval, one does not fall among the various inferior classes; even if born among humans, one is never poor or lowly. Because one upholds the most honored and sublime Dharma, one's person is likewise honored and sublime.
Fourth, the accumulation of all merits:

"Even if these sentient beings themselves do not perform meritorious deeds, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall bestow all their merits upon such a person. By virtue of this, they shall for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—incalculable, unspeakably unspeakable—always be born in the same place as the Buddhas. Their immeasurable merits, like clusters of akṣa fruits, shall be cultivated together in that same place, never to be dispersed."
"Although one may not personally perform meritorious deeds, because of the power of upholding [the teachings], the Buddha bestows merit upon them.
Since they have been born together with him, they continue to receive his instructions and practice accordingly; thus, what merit would not accumulate?"

5. Accomplishment of All Practices. “Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of morality; it causes those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them; it causes those who lack diligence to attain diligence; it causes those who lack wisdom to attain wisdom; it causes those who are impure to quickly attain purity; and it causes those who do not observe the fast and precepts to spontaneously fulfill them.”
"The gateways of the Bodhisattva’s practice are fully realized through actual engagement;
yet now, without such practice, they are nonetheless complete. This is surely due to the power of the divine mantra, which brings all myriad practices to perfection—this statement is not false."
Sixth, the extinction of grave and minor offenses: "Ānanda!

When these good men uphold this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, all offenses of breaking the precepts—regardless of whether they are grave or minor—are simultaneously extinguished after they uphold the mantra. Even if they should drink alcohol or consume the five pungent roots and various kinds of impurities, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, and spirits will not regard this as a transgression."
Even if one wears impure, tattered, and worn-out clothing, whether walking or standing, one is entirely equal to those who are pure.

Even if one does not construct an altar, enter a *maṇḍala*, or practice the Way, yet recites and upholds this mantra, it is no different from the merit of entering an altar and practicing the Way; there is no distinction between them.

If one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, or the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upon reciting this mantra, such grave karma will be completely eradicated—just as a fierce wind blows apart a heap of sand—leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.
"Regarding 'not yet having received it,' this refers to not yet having received the mantra.
The remainder is as in the text.
Seventh, the eradication of past karma."

“Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who, since immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago, have accumulated all manner of light and heavy karmic obstructions, which they have not yet had the opportunity to repent for from previous lives—if they can read, recite, copy, or wear this dhāraṇī upon their bodies, or if it is placed in their dwelling places, houses, gardens, or pavilions—then such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in hot water; before long, they shall all attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
Since births and deaths have been so numerous, how can one calculate the karma created?
Having remained unrepented until now, it all constitutes a heavy obstacle to seeing the Way.
The inconceivable power is like the heat of boiling water; the snow of delusive karma melts away upon encountering it.
Eight, the fulfillment of requests according to one's wishes:

"Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women who have not yet borne sons or daughters and desire to conceive, if they can mindfully recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or wear this *Śītavana-tārā* on their bodies, they will give birth to sons or daughters endowed with merit and wisdom."

Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who desire to swiftly fulfill their karmic rewards shall quickly achieve fulfillment; and the same applies to their physical vitality, strength, and complexion.

"After the end of this life, one will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to one's vows; one will certainly not be born in the borderlands or among the low-born, much less in any hybrid form.
If at the end of life one can still be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas according to one's vows, how much more so for the worldly goals that one seeks—how could they not be attained?
9. Bringing Peace to Their Homes and Nations. "Ānanda!

If in various kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages there be famine, pestilence, or further calamities of war, bandits, strife, and all other lands of misfortune—if one writes out this divine mantra and places it at the four gates of the city, or upon various *caityas*, or atop the *toraṇa* arches, and causes all sentient beings within that land to welcome this mantra with reverence, prostrating and making offerings with a single mind, and causes the people to each wear it upon their persons or place it in their respective dwellings, then all disasters and calamities shall be entirely extinguished."
"Cetiya" means a place worthy of offerings;
"dhvaja" means a banner.
Since [the merit] can even ward off karma, how could it not eliminate minor worldly difficulties? Therefore, they are all extinguished.
10. The Elimination of Obstacles to Abundant Harvests: "Ānanda!

In whatever lands and regions sentient beings possess this mantra, the devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will follow their proper seasons; the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will live in peace and happiness."

Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars and their various transformations according to the directions; calamities and obstacles shall not arise, and no one shall suffer untimely death. Shackles, fetters, and stocks shall not touch their bodies, and they shall sleep peacefully day and night, never experiencing evil dreams.
The five grains refer to hemp, millet, broomcorn millet, wheat, and beans.
Ten billion is called a *zhào*.
Where the Noble Dharma resides, even evil dreams do not occur, let alone other calamities or misfortunes.
11. No Malevolent Stars Enter. "Ānanda!
In this Sahā world, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders."
Furthermore, there are eight great malevolent stars that act as their rulers, manifesting in various forms.
When they appear in the world, they can produce all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings.

"Wherever this mantra is present on the earth, all [calamities] shall be utterly extinguished; for twelve *yojanas* around, it shall become a consecrated boundary (*sīmābandha*) such that no evil omens or disasters can ever enter.
As for the eight great malevolent stars, they are: Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and the comet.
Although there may be auspicious stars, they turn into calamities;
however, where this mantra exists, calamities cannot arise.
Second, the summary indicating the signs of benefit, in two parts:
First, the removal of obstacles and afflictions:

"For this reason, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect all beginners and practitioners in future ages, so that they may enter samādhi with their bodies and minds at ease, attaining great peace and security, and no longer be harmed or afflicted by any demons, ghosts, or spirits, nor by the enmities and calamities from beginningless time, nor by the debts of past karma."
"In this world, there are those whose resolve to practice is earnest yet who encounter many obstacles and afflictions; these are surely the result of past karma.

Even when performing mundane virtues, one encounters many adverse conditions; how much more so for one with a supramundane mind seeking to realize the path of enlightenment? When such a resolve is stirred and set forth, what can possibly oppose it?"
Nothing but the inconceivable power of this secret can dispel [these obstacles].
Second, the attainment of the supernormal power of the mind:

"If you and all those among the assembly who are still in training, as well as all practitioners of future ages, rely upon my mandala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma, and if the precept masters you receive are pure monks, and if you harbor no doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart, then if these good sons do not attain the supernormal power of the mind within this very body born of their parents, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods."

"Penetration of mind" refers to the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*); as previously mentioned, within the first hundred days, those of sharp faculties may attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, which is to say, they attain patience (*kṣānti*) while still in their physical body.

If the superior conditions are complete and one acts according to the Dharma yet fails to attain forbearance, then the Buddha would be a liar; how then could the Tathāgata be one whose words are true?
Third, the protection and maintenance, which has six parts:
first, the Vajra assembly.

When these words had been spoken, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Vajrapāṇis in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall protect with sincere hearts those who thus cultivate bodhicitta."
"The Vajrapāṇi deity, because he protects the Dharma, also protects people.
Second, the assembly of celestial kings.
At that time, the Brahmā King, together with Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings, also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

"If there are such virtuous persons who practice and train in this way, I shall protect them with my whole heart and utmost sincerity, so that all they do throughout their lives may be fulfilled according to their wishes.
3. The Eight Classes of Beings.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, vināyaka great ghost kings, and various ghost commanders who also joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

furthermore, there were immeasurable Sun and Moon Devas, the Master of Wind, the Master of Rain, the Master of Clouds, the Master of Thunder along with the Earl of Lightning, and the officials who cycle through the years, together with the retinues of the various stars, who also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, too, shall protect this practitioner, establish them at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and enable them to attain fearlessness.
The quintessence of yin and yang constitutes the sun and moon;
wind, rain, clouds, and thunder each have their own presiding deities.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable mountain deities and sea deities, as well as the spirits of all lands and the myriad beings that move on land, water, and in the air, along with the Wind Kings and the gods of the Formless Realm.
