"I shall also protect these practitioners so that they attain Bodhi, forever free from demonic interference.
[Thus spoke] the deities of the mountains, rivers, seas, and the five lands.
The celestial deities and terrestrial spirits, as well as those dwelling in space, water, and on land, each have their respective presiding lords, along with various spectral beings.
Sixth, the assembly of the Treasure Kings (Garuḍa Kings) has two parts:
first, an exposition of the intent behind the transformation.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were Kings of the Vajragarbhas, rose from their seats within the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We, having long accomplished our meritorious deeds and realized Bodhi, do not enter Nirvana, but shall constantly follow this mantra to protect and deliver those who cultivate Samādhi and practice correctly during the final age.
"Because compassion increases, one does not enter nirvana; because one protects the Dharma, one constantly follows and upholds the dhāraṇī.
Second, the description of protection and maintenance:
"World-Honored One!"

For those who thus cultivate the mind to seek right concentration—whether they are in a place of practice, walking for meditation, or even when their minds are distracted as they wander through villages—we and our followers shall always follow and attend upon such a person;
even if Māra or Maheśvara should seek an opportunity against them, they shall ultimately find none.
All minor spirits and deities shall remain ten *yojanas* away from these virtuous persons, with the exception of those who have resolved their minds to delight in the cultivation of *dhyāna*.
World-Honored One!

If such evil Māras or their retinues should wish to come and harass these virtuous persons, I shall shatter their heads into fine dust with my precious mallet, and I shall always ensure that whatever these persons undertake is fulfilled according to their wishes.
The sixth [heaven] of the desire realm is named Mahāmaheśvara; it is the abode of Māra, who constantly harasses practitioners so as not to allow them to achieve success.
If one delights in practicing with a virtuous mind, one is not subject to his restrictions; all others are indeed restricted by him.
This great divine mantra is originally the most supreme and excellent condition for those practicing samādhi; therefore, by upholding this mantra, one can repel all evils and gather manifold virtues.
The ignorant and deluded do not understand this principle, and whenever they see one who upholds the mantra, they often give rise to slander, claiming it is not true cultivation.
There has never been a single Buddha who attained the Way or saved sentient beings without relying on this mantra.
As stated above, I request that you examine it closely and reform this deficiency.
The fourth major section, which demonstrates the gradations of the stages, states that once the general practices have been fully understood and internal virtues are completely perfected,
one further relies upon secret mantras to externally augment the power of the path.
The internal and external support one another; how could this be in vain!
It must surely be a matter of sequential stages. Yet, within these stages, there are causes and effects;

delusions have degrees of coarseness and subtlety; wisdom has levels of clarity and obscurity; severance has depths and shallows; realization has partiality and fulfillment; and function has superiority and inferiority. If one is ignorant of this principle, it is not true cultivation, and one falls into the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*).

Because within my teaching, there are differences in the superiority or inferiority of one's progress toward virtue and the cultivation of practice, one gradually enters and deepens through fifty-seven stages; this is unlike the non-Buddhists or celestial Māras, who have no such stages at all.

If one does not discern this in advance, one will deviate from the source as practice progresses; being ignorant of the stages of severance and realization, one mistakenly recognizes a minor attainment and considers it sufficient.
This is like the monk of little learning in the fourth dhyāna who falsely claimed realization, slandered others, and fell into the Avīci Hell.
The matter is not trivial; therefore, it must be clearly explained to avoid incurring great transgression.
The text has two parts:
first, Ānanda’s inquiry, which has two sub-sections: [1a] the request for instruction and [1b] the specific question.
I. Describing the Benefits.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We are dull-witted and fond of much hearing, yet regarding our minds subject to outflows, we have not sought liberation."
"Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, I have attained correct cultivation; my body and mind are refreshed, and I have obtained great benefit.

As for "correct cultivation," it arises from upholding the pure prohibitions and further relying upon secret mantras (*mantra*). Thus, internal demons do not arise and external obstacles do not occur. Cultivating dhyāna by this means, one is free from all deviance and perversity; how great indeed is the refreshing benefit obtained!
2. The Formal Request:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding this cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s samādhi, before reaching nirvāṇa, what are meant by the stage of dry wisdom and the forty-four minds?”
To what gradual sequence does one attain the eye of cultivation?
To what place must one go to be said to have entered the stages (*bhūmi*)?
And what is meant by the term "Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva" (*samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva*)?
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
The great assembly waited with single-minded devotion for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed, unblinking eyes.
Nirvāṇa is the ultimate fruit; it is the destination reached by the stages of realization.
Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is the initial cause, which constitutes the foundational stage of the positions (*bhūmi*).

The forty-four minds—consisting of the stages of faith (*śraddhā*), abiding (*sthiti*), practice (*caryā*), and orientation (*pratipatti*), along with the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*)—constitute the Stage of Practice through Understanding and Resolution (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); this is termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
From the Path of Seeing in the First Ground up to Equal Enlightenment is called "realization and entry," which refers to the fruit of partial realization.

Although Ānanda knew the names of these various grounds, he was unable to discern the meaning underlying those names or the characteristics of their cultivation and realization; therefore, he asked this question. This was to demonstrate his lack of understanding for the sake of future generations.
II. The Tathāgata’s Extensive Exposition, in two parts:
A. Praising the Request and Granting Permission to Teach.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!

You have been able to universally provide for the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future ages who cultivate *samādhi* and seek the Mahāyāna, by revealing from the stage of an ordinary person up to Great Nirvāṇa the unsurpassed path of correct practice.”
"Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms and hollowed their hearts, silently receiving the instruction.
"Hollowing" (刳) means, as it were, making empty.
To empty the body and mind of all miscellaneous thoughts and deliberations, one should attentively receive the meaning of the Dharma.
Second, the correct discernment has two parts:
first, removing delusions that arise regarding the truth.

One falsely establishes the causes for the stages of attainment; however, the arising of these stages fundamentally depends on delusion and enlightenment. Delusion arises from the True, and the fundamental nature is itself void; thus, there are divisions of severance.
The severance itself constitutes awakening; yet as there are degrees of depth in this awakening, there arise successive stages.
Once these stages are distinguished, titles and positions become differentiated. If one were not deluded regarding the Truth, how could such positions exist?
Therefore, it is necessary to provide this narrative.
The text has three parts;
the first is a general exposition of delusion and enlightenment, which has two sub-sections:
First, revealing the single truth.
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks; fundamentally, there have been no worlds and no sentient beings."

The substance of the single truth is profound stillness and perfect luminosity; it is neither true nor false, for names and appearances are entirely extinguished, and the realm of birth and death is thus dissolved.
Since sentient beings and worlds do not exist, who can be named as "Buddha" or "one who has transcended the world"?
Sentient beings delusively discriminate that there are Buddhas and there are worlds.

If one realizes the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there are neither Buddhas nor worlds; this is the single, true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which fundamentally possesses no stages or positions.
2. Exposition of the Two Characteristics:

"Because of delusion there is birth; because of birth there is cessation. Birth and cessation are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called truth. These are termed the two designations for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa as the two transformations of the basis."
The true essence is eternally abiding and fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing.
Failing to realize that the dharma of *tathatā* is one, the mind stirs through non-awakening and gives rise to thought; this thought is precisely the characteristic of arising.

That which arises is immediately subject to cessation; it flows and shifts from moment to moment, gradually becoming coarser until it results in the karmic fruits that circulate through the three realms—therefore, it is called "delusion.

If one recognizes that an evil thought has arisen in the preceding moment and can restrain the succeeding thought so that it does not arise, one will gradually sever coarse afflictions until even subtle afflictions and ignorance are forever exhausted. At the point of ultimate awakening, this is termed "Reality," and herein are established Bodhi and Nirvana.

Regarding the designation of the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): from the initial delusion regarding the Truth where thought moves and proceeds to the cycle of transmigration, it is termed "non-awakening" (*a-vibodha*).
To reverse this non-awakening and realize that there is fundamentally no arising is termed "awakening" (*vibodha*).
This designation "bodhi" is established based on non-awakening.

Because delusion gives rise to birth, and birth must inevitably entail extinction, the reversal of this cycle of birth and extinction reveals that which is neither born nor extinguished; this is precisely the designation "nirvāṇa."

It is established in relation to arising and ceasing; once arising and ceasing have ceased, there is nothing further upon which to rely, and thus it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Taking True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the basis for both delusion and awakening, one transforms this basis of delusion into a basis of awakening, and thus it is called "transformation of the basis."
Thus we know that bodhi and nirvana exist because of delusion, just as the name "awakening" exists because of sleep.
This is likewise the case; it is not that there are originally two distinct fruits within the single, true reality.
Summarizing all stages, there are six kinds of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), as explained elsewhere.
Second, exhorting consciousness to recognize its false causes: "Ānanda!

If you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of delusion regarding sentient beings and the world.
"When inversion does not arise, this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
The preceding section clarified the threefold continuity; here, the two kinds of inversion are clarified.

Since the inversions of sentient beings inherently encompass karma and its fruits, as the previous text states: "If you merely do not follow after the threefold continuity of the world, karma and its fruits, and sentient beings, then because these three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise. Thus, the madness of your inner *Yajñadatta* will naturally subside; this subsiding is itself *bodhi*."
"It is not obtained from others.
Therefore, it is said that the non-arising of inversion is itself true samādhi.
Third, the specific analysis of inversion has two parts:
1. General Exposition of the Causes of Inversion.
"Ānanda, what is meant by the inversions of sentient beings?

Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the mind-nature is perfectly bright, one takes this luminosity as the basis for the arising of the nature; from this, deluded vision is produced, whereby that which is ultimately non-existent becomes that which is ultimately existent."
The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is, by its original nature, true luminosity, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that "the nature is luminously perfect.
From this true luminosity, movement arises from the nature, thereby becoming the characterized (lakṣya).
Once the "object" has been falsely established, the "subjective capacity" arises; this "capacity" is precisely false seeing.
Since both aspects—the subject and the object—do not depart from the True, it is said that "because of clarity, the nature is manifested," and "the nature gives rise to false seeing."
Originally there was only the One True Reality, fundamentally devoid of marks; yet suddenly, through deluded movement, dualistic marks arose abruptly.
From the markless True Reality, the deluded state with marks was formed; therefore, it is said that "ultimate existence is established."
"This is its distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
'This existence possesses that which exists; it is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in an abiding characteristic; it is utterly without root.
This is its common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)."

The aforementioned distinct characteristics (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*) function as the capacity for existence, while the present common characteristics (*sabhāga-lakṣaṇa*) function as that which is possessed.

Although these distinct characteristics were originally non-existent, they arise and serve as the cause for the common characteristics; this is precisely what was referred to in the preceding text as "the cause of such delusion," wherein delusion exists by its own nature.
The subsequent passage also states: "Delusion originally has no cause; within the realm of delusive thought, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions.

Since difference gives rise to sameness, and sameness serves as that which abides while difference serves as that which is abided in, it is therefore called the characteristic of the abider and the abode.

Since this abiding and that which is abided in are fundamentally without cause, what further root could there be? Thus, these two aspects are ultimately without abiding; therefore, it is said that they are utterly without root.
"Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established.
There are no characteristics of identity or difference.
Relying upon the aforementioned identity and difference as the fundamental basis, that which is without identity or difference arises.

The first two characteristics are precisely the substance of the *ālaya-vijñāna* of ignorance; although they are distinguished as being identical or different, in a single thought-moment they transform into subtle arising and ceasing, which is entirely ignorance. From this, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sense organs and bodies, and the seeds all evolve and arise.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because it relies on non-awakening, the mind moves; this is called karma.
Because it relies on movement, there is the capacity for seeing; because it relies on the capacity for seeing, objects falsely appear."
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All phenomena are established based on the root of non-abiding.
This refers to ignorance being without cause; therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
Second, a specific explanation of the meaning of inversion, in three parts:
First, the delusions of sentient beings, in two parts:
1. Delusion due to the appearance of existence.
"Being deluded regarding the fundamental, perfect luminosity gives rise to the false; this false nature has no substance and does not have anything upon which it depends."
This reiterates the characteristics of karma.
By obscuring the true reality of perfect luminosity, one creates the false duality of subject and object.

This deluded movement of subject and object has no fundamental cause or basis; it arises from false conceptualization. Within that which is devoid of identity or difference, a blazing diversity is produced; therefore, it has no substantial essence.
"Desiring to return to the Real, yet that desire for the Real is already not the True Suchness-nature.
This refers to the characteristic of transformation.
Because of the prior movement, the awareness of that movement desires stillness; it detests the delusion and yearns for the Real.

Once desire has arisen, delusion and confusion increase further, and one no longer returns to original stillness; instead, one merely attains a semblance of reality, for this is produced by the transformations of the false and illusory mind. Therefore, it is said that this is not the true Suchness-nature.
"To seek restoration that is not true results in the complete formation of non-characteristics; it is neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor phenomena.
This points to the manifestation of present appearances.
Since they have already become illusory, they are said to be "not true."
When one seeks to return [to the source], the appearance of emptiness manifests; this is precisely the transformation of the true reflection into the various phenomena of the mundane world.
Since the essence of these phenomena is empty, they are said to be "non-phenomena."
"Non-" (*fei*) is synonymous with "false" (*wang*). This is a general enumeration; "non-" serves as the basis for the subsequent detailed listing.

Because that which does not exist suddenly appears, it is called "arising" (*sheng*); because that which exists momentarily ceases, it is called "abiding" (*zhu*); because mental objects continue in succession, it is called "mind" (*xin*); because there are distinctions between defilement and purity, it is called "dharmas" (*fa*); and because their essence is fundamentally unreal, they are all termed "non-."
Among these, "non-mind" refers to the first two of the six coarse states.
Second, receiving birth according to karma:
"Arising through successive succession, the power of birth brings forth manifestation; perfumed by this, karma is formed, and those with identical karma resonate with one another."
"Because there is karmic action born of feeling, one characteristic ceases and another arises; for this reason, sentient beings undergo perversion.
These are the latter four coarse [states].

Because the preceding mind gives rise to discrimination, which gradually becomes increasingly coarse, one grasps and calculates names, thereby creating various karmic actions; thus it is said that "it is perfumed to form karma."

The two karmas of hatred and love each correspond to their respective realms and destinies; karma serves as the cause and retribution as the fruit, resulting in the cycle of mutual arising and mutual extinction.

Because lustful desire acts as the cause, beings arise together; because killing and stealing act as the causes, they mutually perish. This is precisely the twofold continuity of sentient beings and the fruits of karma.
2. The Inversion of the World, in two parts:
1. Explaining the Origination of the World. “Ānanda!
What is meant by the "inversion of the world"?
It is that there is existence where there is nothing, and through the false arising of fragmented [perceptions], this realm is established;
it is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in an abode, but through constant flux and instability, this world is formed.
The three periods of time and the four directions interpenetrate in harmony, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories.
Delusion is ultimately non-existent, yet it constitutes ultimate existence.
Because things exist, the realms (dhātus) are established; because they are distinct and separate, they are called "divisions" (pradeśa).

That which is not a cause acts as a cause, and that which has no abiding dwells [in dependence]. The cause is able to produce the fruit, and the fruit abides within the cause. Cause and fruit produce one another in a continuous flow without interruption; it is by this that the world is established.
The three periods of time and the four directions interpenetrate one another in harmony; these revolutions amount to twelve, and the essence of their transformations is likewise twelve.
Second, the clarification of how delusions arise from one another.

"Therefore, in the world, sound arises from movement; form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form; touch arises from fragrance; flavor arises from touch; and mental objects (dharmas) are known through flavor. Because these six types of deluded conceptualization constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions [of the sense bases] revolve from this."
Therefore, the sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile objects of the world, exhausting twelve transformations, revert as a single cycle.
Internally, due to the characteristic of movement, the external wind-circle is stimulated; thus, sound manifests.
From emptiness arises vibration; when solidity and clarity establish obstruction, form consequently comes into being.
When metal and wind rub against each other, there is fire; from fire comes vapor, and from vapor comes fragrance.

The precious clarity produces moisture, and the fire-light steams upward; from this, flowing water arises. Because the water possesses both cold and warmth, it constitutes the element of touch (*spraṣṭavya*).
Touch is divided into the rough and the smooth; when it encounters the tongue, taste (*rasa*) is produced.
When the five sense objects meet with the mind, they are termed "dharmas.

These six objective realms and the internal faculties' false conceptualizations combine and become entangled; through this, all various karmas are produced, and thus they constitute the nature of karma.
Karma inevitably entails retribution; it is by this that the twelve categories are distinguished, thereby forming the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, the conclusion below establishes "revolving" (*xuanfu*), for revolving is also transmigration.
Sound, odor, taste, and touch represent four out of the twelve [bases].
Third, the classification of types of beings has three parts:
first, the general heading and enumeration.

"Because they ride upon this wheel of inverted characteristics, there are beings in this world born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, and born by transformation; those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; those who are neither with nor without form, and those who are neither with nor without perception."
Sentient emotion and conceptualization cause one another; form and dependency ceaselessly sustain each other. The world of sentient beings does not exceed these twelve categories.

When the first movement of thought arises, one becomes deluded regarding the fundamental, perfect, and eternal nature; consequently, the shadow of illumination appears, and thus egg-birth is placed at the beginning.
Following the arising of emotional attachment, there is subsequently birth from a womb.
Due to differences in attachment and their lack of uniformity, there follow moisture-born and transformationally born beings.
As the mind of perception becomes turbulent, with manifold instances of grasping and rejecting, the subsequent various classes of beings—both those with form and those without form—are formed.
The details will be explained below.
Second, the detailed explanation has twelve parts;
first, the category of movement.

“Ānanda! Because the world revolves through false delusion and is subject to inverted movements, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) gives rise to eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking. Thus, there are egg-born *kalala* beings who circulate through various lands; fish, birds, turtles, and snakes fill these categories.”

The initial emergence of the world originates from falsehood; because it is false, it moves, and this movement is wind, which is breath. Therefore, it is said that it is formed through the harmonious combination of breaths.

Deluded regarding the principle of perfection, permanence, and constancy, one gives rise to false conceptualization; through the convergence of thought and vital energy (*prāṇa*), one is formed within the egg-born mode of birth.
Therefore, the initial stirring of thought constitutes the beginning, and the egg-born state stands at the head.
From this, eighty-four thousand varieties arise; while worldly convention cites this number for the sake of illustration, in principle they are immeasurable.
*Kalala* is here translated as "congealed fluid"; it is the initial stage upon entering the womb, before the embryo and the amnion have differentiated.
Fish, birds, turtles, and snakes are the classes of beings that fly and sink.
Second, the class of desire:

"Due to the inversion of desire within the world’s defiled cycle of rebirth, eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts are formed through conjunction and nourishment; because of this, there is the flow and transformation of *tāyāmbudhama* (embryonic stages) throughout the lands, with humans, beasts, dragons, and immortals filling every category."
Defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); craving is called desire (*kāma*). Because of desire, moisture arises, which is termed "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*).

Regarding "horizontal and vertical": when a person walks the right path, they walk upright with their head raised; because one violates the correct cause and follows the deviant, the horizontal class arises.
"E-putan" refers to the stage of the embryo when the bubble-like mass begins to differentiate into parts.
Third, the category of moisture-born beings:

"Due to the world’s attachment to the cycle of rebirth and its inverted states, the combination of warmth gives rise to eighty-four thousand types of agitated and confused thoughts. Because of this, there are moisture-born beings (*saṃsvedaja*)—embryos in the form of a moist film—that circulate through various lands, teeming with crawling and wriggling creatures that fill every corner."

"Due to attachment, the mind focuses one-pointedly on its object; when it encounters a place of moisture and warmth that corresponds with its perceptions, rebirth occurs immediately—hence it is said that 'warmth completes' [the process].

As for those with inverted and chaotic thoughts, because they act contrary to their own hearts and betray their trust, following their whims and caprices, they consequently experience birth as a class of beings that flies or runs about without stability."
Pīśāca (蔽尸) refers to "soft-fleshed" beings; because they are initially born through moisture, their forms are still supple, and since they do not enter a womb, they lack the preceding stage.
Fourth, the category of *upapāduka* (假類).

"Due to the false inversions caused by the transformation and cyclic flow of the world, the conjunction of contact produces eighty-four thousand types of new and old disordered thoughts. Because of this, there are transformed *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands; those that undergo metamorphosis and those that fly fill the realms."
"Transformation and change are not constant; as the new replaces the old, wherever one encounters an object, it corresponds with perception (*saṃjñā*), and thus birth occurs.

Those whose perceptions are confused by the new and the old do not follow benevolence and righteousness; they loathe the old and grasp for the new, merely following their own passions. Loving that while forgetting this, they rely on what is unreal and undergo transformation into different bodies."

Furthermore, at the initial moment of birth by transformation, the substance is touched by wind and immediately becomes solid; since there is no original form, it is established through this touch. This grasping that transforms and receives a different body is called "transformation" (hua), and is thus termed "metamorphosis" (zhuan-tui).
The *kalala* refers to "hard flesh.
Fifth, the category of obstructions:

"Due to the delusion of obstruction caused by the world’s retention of hindrances within saṃsāra, they combine and adhere to form eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of refined radiance. Because of this, there are *kalala* with physical forms that circulate through the lands; their types, such as those possessing the spiritual brilliance of portents, fill the world."

With obstruction as a condition, there is a barrier that prevents resolution; yet if one encounters something bright and manifest, one clings to it and undergoes birth. This is called the kalala of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

Just as among the stars, planets, sun, and moon, the auspicious are deemed fortunate and the inauspicious are deemed calamitous—even down to the firefly’s spark or the luster of a pearl from an oyster—all belong to this same category.
All of these arise through the transformations of sentient beings, serving as responses to the auspicious or calamitous signs of the world.
Six: The Category of Delusion.

"Because the world’s causes lead to the cycle of deluded inversion and the dissolution of saṃsāra, they combine with darkness to form eighty-four thousand types of obscure and chaotic thoughts. Thus, there exist the formless *kalala* realms of transmigration, filled with those who are dispersed in emptiness or submerged in dissolution."
Taking their dissolution as a condition, they are deluded by darkness and perversion; they loathe and destroy the marks of form and contemplate boundless emptiness.

When form is exhausted and the mind perishes, they grow weary of emptiness and sever all thought, even sinking into the profound obscurity of the Peak of Existence—these are merely the types of non-Buddhists within the Formless Realm.
Seventh, the category of shadows:

"Due to the world's cause of revolving in the void of delusion and the inversion of shadows, the conjunction of memories forms eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts. Because of this, there are the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of thought-forms that circulate through the lands, and spirits, ghosts, and numina of every kind fill these realms."
False images appear as if they exist yet are non-existent; they are efficacious when one believes and recollects them, but not when belief is severed.
Those who merely follow tracks and cling to shadows are all born of conceptualization and recollection.

Consequently, non-Buddhist practitioners and ordinary people pray to deities and offer sacrifices; they preserve their physical forms to establish their spiritual shadows, serving them throughout their lives.
They aspire to supernatural powers, and their spirits are drawn toward and attached to these [deities].
Cause and effect recompense one another; one must be born into their own kind.
Eighth, the class of the deluded:

"Because of the world’s causes of ignorance, dullness, and the cycle of delusive inversion, they combine with stubbornness to form eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts. For this reason, there exist the lands of the non-perceptive *kalala* (embryonic stage) where spirits are transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone, such that these kinds fill the world."
Falling into the mundane world, ignorance serves as its root.
Lacking true awakening, one becomes characterized by dullness and rigidity.

Some may practice meditative concentration until they become like ash or ice, or focus their thoughts until they wither away; yet their minds still shift according to external objects, transforming material things into a physical body.

To take ignorance as true cultivation and to regard stubborn stupidity as the ultimate Way—even such things as the Jiepiluo who transformed into stone, the thousand-year-old flower monuments, and earth-and-wood spirits—all possess a mind that prays for and responds to offerings; they are not ultimately insentient. When their retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth, just as those in the Heaven of No-Thought fall.
9. The Pseudo-Category.

"Due to the delusive inversion of the world’s causal interdependence and cyclic existence, a combination of defilements produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts based on causes. Consequently, there exist non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala* (embryonic stages), circulating through various lands; such as the jellyfish and its kind, which use shrimp as their eyes, filling the world."
"By depending on and relying upon the provisional and the conditional, one is false and unreal.
Entrusting oneself to impurity, one forms a body; borrowing external things, one creates a guide.

This dependence involves a clever fabrication of harmony, altering the old for the new; or by attaching oneself to causes and conditions, mutually leaning upon circumstances to sustain the body and nourish life. Thus the fruits of karma follow one another in succession, just as the *siphonophora* (water mother) forms its body from water foam and uses the shrimp as its eyes."
The eighty thousand families of worms within the bodies of sentient beings all belong to this category.

Having acquired their physical forms by seizing external matter, they subsist on the resources of others; because they do not receive their bodies from their own kind, they are called those "without the characteristics of material form."
Tenth, the Category of Nature:

"Due to the nature of perversion caused by the mutual attraction of the world's phenomena within the cycle of rebirth, they combine with mantras to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning. Because of this, there exist non-formless *kalala* (embryonic stages) that flow through various realms; their kind, produced through curses and incantations, fills the world."
They lead and harmonize one another, inducing them to form their natures.
Curses are further added, summoning them to become their kind.
Although they respond to sounds, it is merely through the mediation of their own inherent natures.
Just as frogs and other such creatures deposit their voices within their eggs before they hatch and grow, and would perish without that sound;

so too, due to an excessive attachment to the realm of sound, or perhaps because of breaking a vow and seeking rebirth through prayers of resentment, one brings calamity upon oneself through mind and speech, and thus reaps the resulting retribution.
Eleven: The Class of Insects.

"Due to the world’s conjunction with delusion and the cycle of inverted transmigration, various combinations produce eighty-four thousand types of confused and chaotic thoughts. Because of this, there arise the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of formative thought from non-existent conditions, which flow and circulate through various lands. Among these, creatures such as the *pulu* (parasitic wasps) are formed by the mutual transformation of different substances; their kind fills the world."

"Through the union of falsehoods, they mutually deceive one another; taking what is different as identical, they turn what belongs to others into their own. Originally lacking any conceptual characteristics, these are later falsely established through appearances—such things as the *pulu* (the cicada) are of this category."
The *púlú* is the *guǒluó* (wasp). It takes green insects as its offspring, which are not born of itself.

By extension, this may represent those who violate filial piety to acknowledge a different duty, abandoning their own root to follow another, erroneously continuing a separate lineage, or falsely assuming the kinship of another clan. As a karmic response, they are reborn as this species.
12. The Category of Killing.

"Due to the cycle of mutual enmity and killing in the world, arising from perversion, beings combine to form eighty-four thousand types who harbor the notion that their parents are food. Consequently, there exist in the realms of transmigration various *kalala* and *arbuda* forms that lack the perception of 'self' or 'other,' such as the earth-owl which fashions its young from clods of earth, and the mirror-cracking bird which nurtures its offspring by clutching the fruit of poisonous trees; once the offspring are formed, both parents are devoured by them, and such species fill the world."
"Vengeful enemies pursue one another in an unceasing cycle.
To entrust such ultimate enmity and slaughter to the relationship of father and son—how strange this is!"

At the initial stage of birth, as they take up their physical form, there is mutual presence of perception and craving; therefore, it is said that they are not without the characteristic of perception.
At a later time, having become fully formed, they encounter being eaten by their parents; therefore, it is said that they are without perception.

The earth-owl breaks mirrors; the earthworm clings to clods of soil and the bird clutches fruit. From generation to generation they succeed one another and inherit this habit; it is karma that causes it to be so, not something natural. Question:
Since these are enemies and adversaries, there can be no principle of being born through mutual resonance. How then can birth occur through clinging, such that there is affection within enmity?
Answer:
Rebirth depends upon the support of craving and attachment, while killing arises from prior karma.
Craving and attachment are impermanent, as they are produced by karma.
Although they initially give rise to affection, it later transforms into hatred; thus, they encounter being eaten.
Third, the classification of names:
"These are called the twelve types of sentient beings."
As in the text.
